title: What If the Moon Was Twice as Close?
next_video: How Long Could You Survive on Every Planet?
voice_style: calm wonder, then brisk for the numbers

beats.text: Imagine stepping outside tonight and seeing a Moon twice as wide as the one you know.
Beautiful. Except every tide on Earth would be pulled {{tide_ratio}} times harder. So what if the Moon was twice as close?
This is The If Engine, where impossible scenarios get real physics, and every number is shown on screen.
Today the Moon orbits about {{d_old_km}} kilometers away, on average. We'll halve that, to {{d_new_km}} kilometers, on a neat circular orbit.
Moving it would not be easy. Bringing the Moon closer means draining energy from its orbit: about {{move_energy}} joules.
That's roughly what the entire Sun radiates into space in {{sun_seconds}} seconds. Not a job for rockets.

visual.label: all of the Sun's output for

beats.text: Here's the strange part. To bring a moon closer, you'd slow it down. It would then fall inward, and end up moving faster than before. Orbits are counterintuitive like that.
So we'll skip the how. Our Moon simply arrives in its new orbit, moving at {{v_new_kms}} kilometers per second instead of {{v_old_kms}}, exactly the speed that orbit needs.
And the first thing anyone would notice is the night sky.
Today the full Moon spans about {{theta_old}} degrees of sky. At half the distance, it spans {{theta_new}} degrees, about twice as wide.

Twice as wide means about {{area_ratio}} times the area. Same sunlight, same dusty gray surface, so the full Moon would shine about {{area_ratio}} times brighter, roughly {{mag_gain}} magnitudes on the astronomer's scale.

It would also race around us. Kepler's third law shrinks the orbit to {{period_new_d}} days instead of {{period_old_d}}. Full Moons would come every {{synodic_new_d}} days instead of every {{synodic_old_d}}.
That means the whole show, from a thin crescent to full and back to dark, would play out in about a week and a half. You'd barely finish one phase before the next began.
Against the stars, it would drift about {{deg_day_new}} degrees a day instead of {{deg_day_old}}. In a single hour, it would slide about {{widths_per_hour}} of its own widths.

visual.title: Drift against the stars, degrees per day

beats.text: And moonrise would slip later each day by about {{moonrise_new_h}} hours, instead of the roughly {{moonrise_old_min}} minutes we're used to.

visual.label: moonrise comes later each day by

beats.text: And from the Moon, the view would change too. Astronauts there would see Earth spanning about {{earth_from_moon_new}} degrees instead of {{earth_from_moon_old}}, a blue world twice as wide hanging over the horizon.
But the real show would happen in daytime. Right now, at its average distance, the Moon looks slightly smaller than the Sun: {{theta_old_precise}} degrees versus {{theta_sun}}.
That's why some solar eclipses today are annular: the Moon doesn't quite cover the Sun, leaving a thin ring of fire around a dark disk.
Twice as close, the Moon would look about twice as wide as the Sun. No more rings. Every central solar eclipse would be total.
And the shadow would be enormous: a dark spot about {{umbra_km}} kilometers across, sweeping over the ground, wide enough to cover a whole country at once.
Now for the part that really matters. Tides don't come from the Moon's pull itself, but from the difference in pull between Earth's near side and its far side.
That difference shrinks with the cube of distance. Halve the distance, and it grows by two cubed: {{tide_ratio}} times stronger.

Notice the twist. The Moon's direct pull on Earth only gets {{pull_ratio}} times stronger, because gravity falls with the square of distance. Tides double that, because they depend on how quickly the pull changes from one side of the planet to the other.
In the open ocean, the Moon's tide today is a gentle bulge about {{bulge_old_cm}} centimeters high, in the idealized case where water responds freely.
Twice as close, that bulge becomes about {{bulge_new_m}} meters, and the swing from high to low tide grows from about {{range_old_cm}} centimeters to about {{range_new_m}} meters.
The timing shifts too. Because the Moon moves faster across our sky, high tide would arrive about every {{tide_period_new_h}} hours instead of every {{tide_period_old_h}}.
But nobody lives in the open ocean. People live at the edges, where the water meets the land.

Real coastlines turn that gentle bulge into something wilder. Bays and gulfs can resonate with the tide, like water sloshing in a bathtub. That's how the Bay of Fundy gets some of the highest tides on Earth.

Harbors, river mouths, wetlands and coastal cities are all shaped around today's tides. Every one of them would be forced by a tide {{tide_ratio}} times stronger, about every {{tide_period_new_h}} hours, without a break.
So how high would Fundy's tides go with {{tide_ratio}} times the push? Honestly, that needs an ocean model, not a calculator. Resonance can amplify or dampen, and the answer changes bay by bay.
What we can calculate is the rhythm. Today the Sun adds a tide about {{sun_share_old_pct}} percent as strong as the Moon's. When they line up, we get extra-high spring tides.

With the Moon twice as close, the Sun's share drops to about {{sun_share_new_pct}} percent. In the simple theory, spring tides today are about {{spring_neap_old}} times the size of neap tides. In the new world they'd be only about {{spring_neap_new_pct}} percent bigger. The monthly rhythm almost vanishes.
Wait. If Earth pulls harder on the Moon too, could the Moon get torn apart?
beats.retention: Open loop: danger to the Moon

beats.text: There is a limit for that, called the Roche limit. Inside it, a moon held together only by its own gravity gets pulled apart by tides. For Earth and our Moon, it's about {{roche_km}} kilometers.
Our new orbit is still about {{roche_margin}} times farther out than that. The Moon would be safe.
Earth would pay a price, though. The tidal bulges drag on our spinning planet like a brake, and that slowly lengthens the day.
This isn't hypothetical physics. The same tidal brake has been slowing Earth for billions of years. It's the reason the day keeps getting very slightly longer.
That braking depends roughly on the Moon's distance to the sixth power. Halve the distance, and it gets about {{brake_ratio}} times stronger.
Tidal friction should be adding about {{lod_old_ms}} milliseconds to the day every century. Twice as close, that becomes about {{lod_new_ms}} milliseconds per century.
Over a million years, that's about {{myr_new_min}} extra minutes per day instead of about {{myr_old_s}} seconds, if the rate stayed constant, which it wouldn't exactly.

There's a flip side. The same tidal tug that slows Earth also pushes the Moon gently outward. Our real Moon is drifting away by about {{recession_cm}} centimeters a year. A closer Moon would be pushed outward harder, slowly undoing part of our experiment.

And you? Would you feel lighter with that giant Moon overhead? For a {{person_mass}} kilogram person, the extra tidal pull changes your weight by about {{weight_new_g}} grams. That's less than a tenth of a gram.

Today it's about {{weight_old_g}} grams. Tides need size to work. Across Earth's {{earth_diam_km}} kilometers, the Moon's pull changes enough to lift whole oceans. Across a human body, the difference is far too small to feel.

So, a Moon twice as close: about {{area_ratio}} times brighter, a full Moon every {{synodic_new_d}} days, only total eclipses, tides {{tide_ratio}} times stronger, and days stretching about {{brake_ratio}} times faster.
Distance is the quiet number behind our sky, our oceans, and even the length of our days. Change it by half, and almost everything we take for granted about the Moon changes with it.
Every number here came from a calculation or a cited source, all listed in the description. Check our math.
Next time, we leave Earth entirely: how long could you survive on every planet in the solar system? Subscribe so you don't miss it. This was The If Engine. Run the impossible. Do the math.

metadata.hook: Halve the Moon's distance and it looks twice as wide. Every tide on Earth gets {{tide_ratio}} times stronger.
metadata.summary: We run the scenario through real physics with every calculation on screen: the new sky, a {{synodic_new_d}}-day lunar month, eclipses that are always total, equilibrium tides, the Roche limit, tidal braking and whether you'd feel it.
